msItem.incipit: Twas not my fate to see thee (noble lord)

abstract.p: This elegiac poem laments the death of Dr. Searchfield, Bishop of Bristol, from the perspective of a speaker who arrived too late to see him alive or attend his funeral, offering instead a belated poetic tribute. It presents his death as untimely—like a sun setting at noon—while also affirming that his soul now shines more brightly in heaven. The poem then turns into a sharp critique of Bristol, initially condemning its citizens as a whole but more pointedly targeting the city’s religious and civic structures: the local clergy—especially those of a puritanical, anti-episcopal bent—are satirized as ignorant, factious, and hostile to church authority, while the civic authorities are implicated in enabling and sustaining this environment through their control over appointments and patronage. In such a climate of “senseless broils,” the bishop is effectively worn down and driven to an early death. In contrast, Searchfield is praised as a model prelate—grave yet gracious, devoted to his duties, and committed to reforming the Church—whose virtue was recognized only by the discerning few, making his loss both a personal tragedy and a wider indictment of the society that failed him.

div.head: On Dr Searchfeild Bishopp of Bristoll Oct 21 1622

lg.l: ‘Twas not my fate to see thee (Noble Lorde)
Nor did I to thy funeralls afforde a personall observance
A personall observance; No; I spedd
For all my hast but thus to finde thee deade
Take then this Posthumus dutye, though thy herse
Can reape no honour from my simple Verse;
Nor did from the drie Sermon: Dr Chettwine, Deane of Bristell yet I crave
This leave to sobb a sadd Dirge ‘ore thy grave.
Did I for this so long too see thy Towers
Farr famed Bristoll? Did I chidd the howers,
That barrd mee from thy wished sight, for this
This mournfull welcome? Hence forth shalt thou misse
Thy visitants, if the first night thou use
To entertaine thy guest with such badd news.
And yett I blame thee not; thy sadd array
Became thy state, for night had seiz’d the day:
Thy glorious Sunne wente downe in his high noone.
Why did hee mount so high to sett so soone.
So soone, as though hee only strove to gett
Unto those Westerne parts that hee might sett.
And yett though sett he shines, and shines and shinn most bright
(Which is most strange), now Hee’s deprived of light;
His soule having scap’t her prison, now displaies
Her brightest lustre; and resplendant raies:
Leaving us heere to see itts worth and moone,
Being (like great Goods) now Hee’s lost best knowne
But I must sett my notes to a new Song,
And wonder how hee could live heere so long
Mongst such scumme of people, a base crue,
Unworthy of his worth give them theire due,
Most naturall Citizens, who could bee content
To have the meanes, where ere the Bishopp went:
And this Bristoll pure in all save sinne
A priviledg place to kill a Bishopp in.
I only wish (pleas’d itt the King and State)
They bought theire Prelatts att a higher rate;
For they intend to kill upp more I feare,
Then that will buy three hundred pounds The valew of that Bishopprick 3 or 4 hundred poundesso deare.
Tis meanes enough to starve an honest man;
Yett they have surer waies wherby they can
Kill safer then Phisitions; A new art
By scensles broyles to breake a Bishopps heart.
They have a goodly cleargy to, wh weare all knowne,
Except some few whom they dare scarsly owne,
Who still when new teachers to them are putt
Trimme ‘em them att Cytty charge ‘oth of the Puritann cutt;
And who ere meanes his freind heere to preferre;
Hee must bee a thus qualified minister.
Can hee att a bordes end screw upp his face
And cole the brooth with a long winded grace.
Is hee an obstinate asse? and will hee snapp
A Bishopps Rochett rochet , or his corner’d capp?
Will not his conscience with Church-Rites dispence?
And doth hee zelously snuffell upp non-scence?
Can hee with skill knocke sound wordes out joynt?
Draw fifteene uses from the fourteenth poynt?
Eats hee large meales can he new doctrines hatch,
And teach the King to weild the Spanish match?
Hates hee all Gentlemen? And the Latine Toungue
Cause tis the Romane Language? will hee wronge
Any for his owne endes? And lastly dare
Traduce all Governours but Mr Mayor?
Bee wise send him to Bristoll when hee’s heere;
Hee’s in Election for tenn poundes a yeare,
And tis faier too: Make much on’t when tis suer,
Heele scarse deserve a twenty Nobles cure.
Oh who would live so subject to the hate
Of such base vermine; where itt not the fate
Of greatnesse, to bee still by envy knowne
And when tis trodden most to rise best growne.
So was the Noble Prelatt still withstood
Yett sacrefised him selfe to’th Churches good:
Only the wise, and Gentry found his worth,
And finding lov’d itt thus sent him foorth
In his trew coulours, that hee was belov’d
Of such whose wisdome knew why they approv’d:
For theire discerning eies without the booke,
Might reade a Noblenesse in his verie looke,
Hee was of grave aspecte of a severe
Yett Gentle carriadge, gesture debonaire,
A winning conversation to the end,
Hated all ill and truly lov’d his freind
How carefull of his charge, his living heere
(Though with his losse) can witnesse! Three full yeare
Hee spente him selfe to mende the Churches state,
And for his pains his best reward was hate.
So that impatient of not doing well good
As being ill Consterd or not understood
Hee flew from to Heaven as voyde of guilt or feare
To make the auditt of his actions theere.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: During Bishop Searchfield’s tenure at Bristol (1619–1622), the city’s civic authorities exercised significant control over ecclesiastical matters and were resistant to episcopal initiatives. In 1620, when Searchfield supported a proposal to increase the incomes of Bristol’s ministers, the city corporation refused to cooperate and opposed the measure, even when it was backed by the Privy Council. This episode illustrates the limited scope of episcopal authority within the city and the strength of civic control over church affairs, tensions which are reflected in the poem’s portrayal of Bristol as a hostile environment for its bishop. (Harlow 2017)
